desc:
Choose two non-empty subsets A and B of the positions of nums such that they share no position and the sum of the values in A equals the sum of the values in B. The pair is ordered: swapping the roles of A and B gives a different pair, and different positions with equal values count as different choices.

Return the number of such pairs modulo 1,000,000,007.

For [1, 2, 3] the pairs are A = {1, 2}, B = {3} and the swapped pair, so the answer is 2.
hints: Give every element one of three roles: in A, in B, or in neither. That is 3<sup>n</sup> assignments, too many for n = 30.
You never need the two sums separately, only their difference sum(A) - sum(B). Count assignments per difference value.

Keep a table ways[d]. For each element x, an assignment with difference d moves to d (neither), d + x (in A) or d - x (in B). Because all values are positive, equal sums with A non-empty force B to be non-empty, so only the empty-empty assignment must be removed from ways[0].
editorial: Count assignments of every position to {A, B, neither} by the difference d = sum(A) - sum(B). The differences lie in [-S, S] with S = sum(nums) ≤ 1,800, so a table (or hash map) of at most 3,601 entries is enough, updated once per element with the three transitions above. The total work is about 30 · 3,601 · 3 updates.

At the end ways[0] counts every assignment with equal sums. That includes the assignment where nothing is chosen at all. Since all values are positive, a non-empty A has positive sum, so B has positive sum and is non-empty as well, and the reverse holds too; hence the only invalid assignment with difference 0 is the all-neither one, and the answer is ways[0] - 1 modulo 109+7. Backtracking over 3n assignments is only a viable brute force for very small n; the difference table removes the exponential.
